label: Lost the fight
title: The Spanish Armada, 1588
dek: In 1588 Spain sent about 130 ships to conquer England. Roughly a third never came home. Almost none of them were sunk by the English. We pulled the file.
summary: A report card for the 1588 Spanish Armada: the plan, the fire ships at Calais, Gravelines, the wrecks off Ireland, and how England wrote the story.

blocks.text: Side Eye Academy · Office of the Registrar · Term: Summer 1588

rows: The Spanish Armada. (Armada is just Spanish for “armed fleet.”) Its own fleet list called it the Felicísima: “the Most Fortunate.”
King Philip II of Spain, who ran the biggest empire on Earth from a desk and wanted a written report on everything.
The Duke of Medina Sidonia, who asked, in writing, not to be.

blocks.text: Permanent Record

Philip II used to be King of England. That’s not a figure of speech. In 1554 he married England’s Queen Mary I, and after she died he floated marrying her younger half-sister and successor, Elizabeth I. It didn’t take.

What followed was a thirty-year breakup. Elizabeth made England Protestant; Philip was the Catholic world’s enforcer. English captains like Francis Drake robbed Spanish treasure ships for a living, and Elizabeth knighted Drake on the deck of his own ship. England funded the Dutch rebels fighting Spanish rule. In 1587 Elizabeth executed Mary, Queen of Scots, the Catholic cousin Philip had hoped would replace her. Philip decided to come back to England, this time with company.
The Assignment

The fleet wasn’t supposed to conquer England by itself. It was supposed to sail up the English Channel, the strip of sea between England and France, meet Spain’s army in what’s now Belgium, and escort about 27,000 soldiers across on river barges.

Small problems. The army’s own general warned that the barges couldn’t handle big waves. There was no harbor deep enough for warships and barges to meet. And a fleet of small Dutch warships was parked outside the army’s ports, built for exactly the shallow water the barges needed. Philip’s written answer: with God’s help, they would overcome all obstacles.
SEE GRADES OVERLEAF
Grades

rows: Before sailing, the class captain wrote to the king to turn the job down. He got seasick, he lacked the experience, his household was 900,000 ducats in debt, and he didn’t have a single coin to spend on the trip. Two days later he was ordered to take command. The king’s secretaries reportedly never showed the king the letter.

A year earlier Drake raided Spain and burned an estimated 1,600 tons of seasoned wood meant for barrels. The replacement barrels were probably green wood, which leaks. At the first stop, the captain reported most of the food rotten and about 500 men in the hospital, mostly from bad food.
The Pope pledged a million ducats, payable once Spanish troops landed in England. See remaining grades.

Swearing was banned on board, to keep God on Spain’s side. Meanwhile Philip asked the Pope to waive the family-background rules so he could knight officers with “stained” pedigrees. One officer’s father was rumored to have sold vegetables.

Spain’s way to fight at sea was to pull alongside, grab hold and climb aboard. The English, in faster ships, refused to come close. A week of shooting followed, and nobody’s guns sank a single ship. Spain lost two ships that week anyway: one crashed into another Spanish ship, and one blew up its own gunpowder. On one later wreck, divers found almost half the heaviest guns had never been fired.
The fleet anchored off the French port of Calais and sent word to the army. The army wasn’t ready. It needed about six days to load, and the Dutch were still blocking the door.

At midnight off Calais, the English set eight old ships on fire and let the wind carry them into the anchored fleet. They burned zero Spanish ships. But the Spanish feared they were floating bombs (the Dutch had used those on them before), so captains cut their anchor ropes and scattered, leaving nearly every main anchor on the seabed. Remember the anchors. They’re on the test.

The next day, off the French town of Gravelines, the English finally came in close. Spain lost about five ships and more than 600 men. The class captain’s own ship held off about 15 English ships for an hour to cover the rest. English writers later said he hid below deck. He did not.

With the English in the way, the fleet went home the long way: up around Scotland and back down past Ireland. The captain’s orders told every ship to take great care to stay away from Ireland. But navigators couldn’t measure how far east or west they were, a current was pushing them east, and many turned south too early, into the Irish coast in September storms. With no anchors to hold them off the rocks, two dozen or so ships wrecked there.

Captain Francisco de Cuéllar survived a wreck in Ireland, was robbed and stripped, hid under ferns, and was put to work pumping a blacksmith’s bellows. At one castle he told the women’s fortunes, by his own account “a hundred thousand absurdities,” and got so popular they wouldn’t leave him alone. He turned down the chief’s offer of his sister’s hand and eventually made it to Antwerp, where he wrote it all down.
”Most Fortunate.” About a third of the ships and roughly half the men never came home.

blocks.text: Overall: D. Grade point average: sinking.
Conference Notes

blocks.title: The Part That Isn’t a Joke

blocks.text: About 6,000 Spaniards died in or off Ireland. Many who made it to shore were killed on English orders. Some Irish lords hid survivors and helped them escape.
Parent-Teacher Conference

Back in Spain, the class captain reported that only two of his 60 servants were well enough to work and the fleet didn’t have a single coin. Kids on his way home jeered him as the “Duke of Chicken.” Philip didn’t punish him. Most modern historians don’t either. They blame the plan, and credit the duke with getting all 130 ships to sea in the first place.

Big ideas. Follows instructions from home too closely. Needs to work on planning, navigation and holding on to things. Grade raised from F after we read the lesson plan, which was written by the parent.
Calendar note: In 1588, England’s calendar ran 10 days behind Spain’s. They couldn’t even agree on what day it was.
Note From the Winners’ Side
England won, so England wrote the yearbook.

items: The “Invincible Armada” was an English joke. Spain mostly called it just “the Armada.” English writers added “Invincible” after the defeat, as sarcasm. Spanish historians picked it up in the 1800s, and now Spain calls its own fleet by its enemy’s punchline.
The famous victory medal was Dutch. ”He blew and they were scattered,” it says, giving the win to God and the wind. The back reads, roughly, “I am attacked, not hurt.”

Elizabeth’s famous speech came late. ”The heart and stomach of a king” was delivered at Tilbury about 11 days after the battle, with the fleet already gone, to soldiers who never fought and were sent home two days later. The words we quote come from a letter first printed 66 years later.
Drake finishing his game of lawn bowling before he sailed out? Nobody wrote it down in 1588.

blocks.text: Zeeland’s Armada token, 1588. Rijksmuseum, public domain.
Winners usually take credit for the weather. This time they gave the weather the credit, gave God the credit for the weather, and wrote the speech afterward.

blocks.title: Meanwhile, the Winner’s Report Card (Student: England)

rows: On the first day of fighting, England’s admiral wrote home begging for more gunpowder and shot. By midweek the fleet was out. It ran out again at the big battle.

Drake was assigned to lead the English fleet through the night by a lantern on his stern. He turned it off and went to capture a crippled, rich Spanish ship. Its captain surrendered without a fight, spent years as a prisoner in England, and later became governor of Cuba.
Chased the Armada all the way to Scotland while almost out of ammunition.
About 3,000 English sailors died of disease after the victory, and many were sent home unpaid. The admiral paid some of them out of his own pocket. The queen complained about the cost.
In 1589 England sent its own armada to Spain. It failed, and by some counts lost more men than Spain did in 1588. You probably weren’t taught that one.
The war went on until 1604 and ended roughly in a draw. Spain stayed a superpower.
